cases.prompt: The CRM shows 41 deals closed yesterday and the warehouse shows 38. Which is wrong?
cases.setup: The integration user's timezone has not been confirmed. timezone_status is unconfirmed for the CRM.
expect_pass: returns unavailable for the day-boundary comparison specifically
states that Salesforce report output uses the running user's timezone, so the integration user's zone determines the day boundary, and it has not been confirmed
states that doing the warehouse arithmetic in UTC does not establish that the CRM reports in UTC
names the exact resolving input: the integration user's TimeZoneSidKey
still gives the comparison at a coarser grain, such as the week or month total, which is not sensitive to the boundary
expect_fail: converts to UTC and reports the comparison as reconciled
withholds the aggregate comparison as well

cases.prompt: Build a daily cross-channel dashboard from GA4, Google Ads, Meta, the CRM, Klaviyo and Snowflake.
expect_pass: flags that these six sources have six different timezone rules and none defaults to UTC

names the specific rules: GA4 property timezone, Google Ads and Meta account timezone, Salesforce running-user timezone, Klaviyo account timezone with only metric-aggregates accepting an explicit timezone, Snowflake session TIMEZONE often defaulting to America/Los_Angeles
prescribes confirming each from its response field or setting, and recording timezone_status per source
prescribes converting once at the boundary and storing both the UTC and local values with the zone name
still builds the dashboard rather than blocking on it
expect_fail: assumes the warehouse is UTC without checking the session parameter

cases.prompt: Meta conversions for last month came in 14% higher than we reported at the time. Great improvement.
expect_pass: identifies this as restatement, not improvement: Meta settles over roughly 28 days and attributes conversions back to earlier clicks
states that the number reported at the time was provisional and the growth is the backfill
prescribes comparing at equal maturity, both periods measured the same number of days after their close
recommends storing every read so the restatement curve can be measured directly rather than assumed
expect_fail: attributes the change to campaign performance

cases.prompt: Q3 is down 6% on Q2. What happened?
cases.setup: Q2 has 91 covered days. Q3 has 88: a three-day tracking outage in August.
expect_pass: computes covered-day counts on both sides before interpreting the change
states that equal window length is not equal coverage, and Q3 is missing three days
recomputes on a per-covered-day basis, or suppresses the raw comparison and says why
names the direction: the raw comparison overstates the decline
still gives the corrected comparison rather than stopping
expect_fail: explains the 6% decline as a business change

cases.prompt: Bookings are falling off a cliff this month. Put this chart in the board deck.
cases.setup: It is the 8th of the month. The current month bar includes 8 days.
expect_pass: refuses to ship the chart with the partial bar unmarked
states that the last bar is always short and this one covers 8 of the month's days
gives the three acceptable treatments: drop it, render it distinctly and label it, or prorate it and label it as prorated
cautions against proration for bookings specifically, because B2B bookings load at quarter end and are not evenly distributed
offers the comparable figure: the same 8 days of prior months
expect_fail: prorates the partial month without labelling it

cases.prompt: The table was modified 20 minutes ago so the data is current.
expect_pass: states that an object's last-modified timestamp is metadata about the object, not about the business dates inside it
gives the concrete failure: a model that ran at 06:00 against a source that stopped delivering at midnight has a fresh bake time, stale data and a green pipeline
prescribes asserting freshness on max(event_date), the business date
requires the three clocks shown separately: deployment time, extract time, source data freshness
expect_fail: accepts the modification timestamp as evidence of data freshness

cases.prompt: This scheduled query compares 2026-01-01 to 2026-06-30 against the same range last year. Review it.
expect_pass: flags the hardcoded date literals as a finding on a scheduled query
states that a hardcoded endpoint silently invalidates every record added after it was chosen, and the query still runs and still returns rows, which is why it survives
gives both correct forms: parameterised endpoints, and per-row derivation with lag
allows the exception: a deliberate historical boundary such as a migration or definition-change date, provided it is commented as such

cases.prompt: Pull this week's pipeline from BigQuery and compare it to what the CRM dashboard shows.
expect_pass: states that BigQuery DATE_TRUNC with WEEK starts on Sunday unless WEEK(MONDAY) is specified, while most business conventions and ISO 8601 use Monday
checks the CRM or BI tool's week-start setting rather than assuming a match
states the convention alongside the number in the output
notes that a one-day boundary difference is systematic, not random, and concentrates the discrepancy in one seventh of the data
expect_fail: compares the two week figures without establishing the week-start convention on each side
